name: Dockproof — per-PO pre-ship compliance gate and evidence packet for retail suppliers
one_liner: For the retail operations manager at a $5M-$100M CPG brand (and the 3PL account manager who ships for them), Dockproof turns each retailer's routing guide plus the brand's own chargeback history into a per-PO pre-ship checklist that must be cleared before the truck leaves — and files the cleared checklist, label scans and photos as a dated evidence packet that wins the dispute if a deduction lands anyway.
problem: A CPG brand shipping to Walmart, Target, Kroger, Costco or Amazon is judged against a 50-150 page routing guide/vendor manual per retailer, revised on each retailer's own schedule and published quietly to a portal (Retail Link, Partners Online, Vendor Hub). Violations — wrong carrier, missed delivery window, ASN late or mismatched, carton label placement, pallet build, case-pack accuracy — are deducted straight off the remittance. Secondary industry sources put Walmart OTIF at 3% of cost of goods on non-compliant cases, Target ASN fees at $0.75/carton with a $100 minimum, and routing violations at $50-$500 per shipment; Credit Research Foundation benchmarks put non-trade deductions at a median 1.1-2% of sales, and vendor sources put total deductions far higher. Today the brand's ops manager holds the rules in their head, a PDF folder and a spreadsheet, the 3PL holds the physical execution, and the EDI provider only validates document syntax — so nobody owns the pre-shipment check. When a deduction lands, the brand (or a recovery vendor) spends days assembling BOLs, ASN timestamps, label records and pallet photos after the fact, often fails, and then ships the exact same error next week because the deduction code was never translated into a fix.
target_customer: Primary buyer: the Director of Retail Operations / Supply Chain Manager at a CPG brand doing $5M-$100M wholesale across 3-20 retail accounts — the person whose number is "deductions as % of sales" and who already approves spend on EDI ($500-$4,200/mo range per CPG industry estimates) and deduction recovery. Secondary buyer and best distribution channel: the client-services or compliance lead at a retail-focused 3PL running 20-80 retail accounts across several facilities, who eats disputed chargebacks and wants neutral proof of what shipped.
why_now: Three things changed. (1) Document parsing got good enough to turn a 120-page routing guide into structured, source-cited rules — LlamaIndex shipped the Document Parsing Protocol on 28 Oct 2026 with 140 rules specifically covering tables, forms, checkboxes and key-value regions, the exact structures routing guides are made of (https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/introducing-the-document-parsing-protocol), and a16z's Big Ideas 2026 names "startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" as a 2026 theme (https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/). (2) Retailer rules moved again in 2026: Target's SPM compliance policy update reportedly took effect 3 May 2026 adding physical case-pack accuracy and DC item-attribute audits, Walmart began collecting shipment-level food traceability data, and a new Amazon PO-accuracy chargeback code (CB-1147) was reported effective 15 Apr 2026 — each a forced re-read of the manual (dates from secondary sources; verify in the retailer portals). (3) Investor aim: YC's latest RFS "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert) describes exactly this shape — a warehouse supervisor backed by AI doing work that today needs a retail-compliance specialist — and a16z's "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" points at non-Valley operators as the 2026 buyer (https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-2/).
comparables: SPS Commerce (spscommerce.com) — the EDI incumbent, sells fulfillment EDI plus a Revenue Recovery product and claims preventive compliance monitoring with vendor-reported 20-40% chargeback reduction; reviews on G2/Capterra/Trustpilot complain about cost, billing for unused services, slow support, and mapping errors that themselves cause chargebacks. Gap: it is a document pipe, not a dock gate — it validates EDI syntax, not whether the pallet actually matched the guide. SupplyPike (supplypike.com, $25M Series B 2022, ~$40M total, flat fee on shipping volume), iNymbus (~$0.40-0.70/claim), Glimpse (tryglimpse.com), Vendormint, RetailPath ($1.3M pre-seed, Gutter Capital), AisleCore ($749-$1,699/mo) — all recovery-side: they validate and dispute deductions after they post. Gap: none of them, on the public evidence, closes the loop from a deduction code back to a check on next week's PO. RetailerHub (retailerhub.ai) is the closest and the real competitor: founded 2024, 1-10 people, bootstrapped, $500-$3,000/mo, uploads routing guides into searchable SOPs with a "Version Intel" change-diff feature. Gap: its own positioning stops at SOPs and alerts — it does not gate a specific PO, does not ingest the brand's deduction history, and does not produce a shipment-level evidence packet. Cleo launched a "Chargeback Prevention" feature flagging at-risk orders (EDI-centric, enterprise). Crstl (Shopify Ventures-backed) validates EDI against retailer profiles. ShipMonk offers timestamped freight loadout photos for its own 3PL clients only. Honest read: the category is busy, but it is split between document pipes, SOP libraries and recovery tools; the per-PO gate + evidence packet sits in the seam.
market_note: Estimates, labelled as such. Kroger alone reports 60,000+ vendors and suppliers (broad definition, not brand count); there is no clean public count of CPG brands selling into Walmart/Target. A defensible bottom-up: ~15,000-30,000 US brands in the $5M-$100M wholesale band with multi-retailer exposure (estimate). At $500-$1,500/month — the band RetailerHub actually publishes ($500 for 1-5 retailers up to $3,000 for 76-100) and below AisleCore's $749/$1,699 tiers — a 1,500-customer business is roughly $18M ARR. Willingness to pay is anchored not on software budget but on avoided deductions: for a $20M brand, 1-7% of sales in deductions is $200K-$1.4M/yr (directional vendor/industry estimates), so a $12K/yr tool only needs to stop a handful of OTIF or ASN events. The 3PL channel multiplies this: one 3PL with 60-70 retail accounts (GPA Logistics, per RetailerHub's case study) is a single sale covering dozens of brands.
risks: 1) The seam may be a seam for a reason: the brand feels the deduction but the 3PL controls the dock, so the product needs cooperation from two parties to actually block a shipment — if it degrades to "another dashboard the brand reads," value collapses to RetailerHub's $500/mo SOP tier. 2) Incumbent reach: SPS and Cleo already sit in the data path and are adding prevention features; they can bundle a per-PO check for free. 3) Data access is grubby — deduction reports mostly come out of Retail Link / Partners Online / Vendor Central as manual portal exports with no public API, and ASN data lives with the EDI provider or 3PL WMS; a lot of forward-deployed plumbing per customer, which is slow for an evenings-and-weekends builder. 4) Evidence packets only pay off if retailers actually accept them; dispute win rates are vendor-reported.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That the pre-ship moment is buyable: someone (ops manager or 3PL supervisor) will actually hold a shipment on a red check, rather than treating the output as advisory. If not, the product is an SOP library and RetailerHub already owns that at $500/mo. 2) That mapping a retailer's deduction codes back to specific, checkable pre-ship conditions is reliably doable from the guide + the brand's own chargeback history — my research found this workflow described as feasible and recommended, but found no vendor proving it end to end. 3) That a brand will pay $1,000-$1,500/mo on avoided-loss logic without a clean attribution story, given deductions are noisy and partly out of their control (carrier, retailer error).
first_customers: Ten named targets, reachable this month: (a) 5 emerging CPG brands in the $10M-$40M band with 4+ big-box accounts — find them in the SPS Commerce "SupplierWiki" webinar attendee community, the r/CPG and Foodboro/Startup CPG Slack channels, and Expo West / Fancy Food exhibitor lists; the person to email is the Director of Retail Ops or the one-person "Vendor Compliance Manager" (live listings exist, e.g. ZWILLING J.A. Henckels, Just Ingredients Sr. Retail Operations Manager with chargebacks and scorecards explicitly in scope). (b) 3 retail-focused 3PLs — Taylor Logistics, ODW Logistics, Buske, Atomix, GPA Logistics all publish retail-compliance content, meaning they sell compliance as a differentiator and feel the liability; pitch the client-services lead. (c) 2 deduction-recovery firms (Vendormint, Glimpse-type managed services) as white-label partners — they see root causes daily and have no prevention product to upsell.
validation_test: This week, free, no code: ask 8 CPG ops managers and 3 retail 3PLs for (i) their current routing guide PDF for one retailer and (ii) a CSV of their last 90 days of deductions. Turn one of them around in 48 hours by hand (with Claude + the DPP rules) into a one-page per-PO pre-ship checklist for their next three POs, with each line citing the page of the guide and tagged with the deduction code it prevents. Pass signal: 3 of 11 send both files, and at least 2 ask you to run it on their next real shipment or ask what it costs. Hard pass signal: they read it, say "useful", and will not give you a live PO — that means the gate is advisory, not operational, and the idea should be reshaped toward the 3PL as the buyer.
build_plan: Narrowest first version — one retailer (Walmart), one brand, one shipment type. 1) Guide-to-rules: ingest a routing guide / vendor manual PDF with a parser following LlamaIndex's DPP conventions; emit a structured rule set (ship window, carrier/routing, carton + SSCC label spec, pallet build, ASN fields and timing, case-pack) where every rule carries a page citation. Human-review the extraction — do not pretend it is fully automatic. 2) History-to-risk: take a CSV of the brand's last 90 days of deductions, normalise reason codes, and rank which rules this brand actually fails. 3) The gate: a per-PO checklist screen — paste or upload the PO plus the planned ASN/pack data, get pass/fail per rule, red items blocking sign-off, each with the guide citation and the dollar exposure if missed. 4) The packet: on sign-off, freeze a dated PDF with the checklist, the ASN timestamp, label scans and dock photos uploaded from a phone — this is the dispute evidence and the reason the 3PL cooperates. 5) Version Intel parity: re-parse the guide monthly, diff it, and show only rules that changed and which checks they affect. Cut for v1: EDI transmission, WMS/ERP integration, auto-dispute filing, multi-retailer coverage, any attempt to replace SPS. Sell it as a $1,000/mo pilot to one brand plus its 3PL, run forward-deployed for the first three customers.
reasoning: Dockproof won because it is the only candidate where I found a named role whose job title is the problem ("Vendor Compliance Manager", live listings), a recurring weekly cost with published dollar mechanics (3% of COGS on Walmart OTIF cases, $0.75/carton Target ASN fees, $50-$500 routing violations, 1.1-2% of sales median non-trade deductions per CRF), an active buying market proving budget exists (SupplyPike's $25M Series B, RetailPath's $1.3M pre-seed, AisleCore at $749-$1,699/mo, RetailerHub at $500-$3,000/mo), and a workflow step that all of those players visibly skip. The research kept pointing at the same split: SPS and Cleo are document pipes, RetailerHub is an SOP library, SupplyPike/Glimpse/iNymbus/RetailPath are recovery. Nobody on the public evidence closes the loop from a posted deduction code back to a blocking check on next week's PO, with the evidence frozen at the dock. That seam is the whole company. It builds on no past library idea — the closest is Backcheck (also a "painful PDF becomes a compliant package" shape) but the buyer, document, workflow and industry are entirely different: permit coordinator vs retail ops manager, plan-check letter vs routing guide, resubmittal vs shipment release. Honest marks against it: gap stays at 7 because RetailerHub is genuinely close and I could not verify how far its SOPs go toward per-PO enforcement, and timing stays at 7 because the 2026 Target/Amazon rule-change dates came from secondary sources I could not confirm in the retailer portals. Pain is latent-adjacent on one dimension — brands clearly complain about deductions, but almost nobody today frames the problem as "we have no gate at the dock", so the first conversations have to lead with their own deduction report, not with the product. Investor signals used as aim, not as evidence: YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (an ordinary warehouse supervisor doing specialist compliance work) and a16z's "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" plus "startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" all point here, but the score rests on the deduction numbers and the competitor map, not on the signals.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Dockproof — per-PO pre-ship compliance gate + evidence packet for CPG brands and their 3PLs. PICK. Named buyer with a deductions KPI, recurring weekly pain with real dollar figures, and a seam between EDI pipes, SOP libraries and recovery tools.
2. Routing-guide change monitor (alert suppliers when a retailer revises a manual) — finalist, folded into Dockproof as a feature. Lost standalone: RetailerHub's "Version Intel" already does exactly this at $500/mo, so it is a feature, not a company.
3. Deduction-code root-cause analytics for CPG — dropped at deep research. SupplyPike ($40M raised), iNymbus, Glimpse, RetailPath, AisleCore ($749-$1,699/mo) crowd the recovery side; a pure analytics layer has no wedge against them.
4. Shop-floor/back-office agent for small manufacturers (off Faraday YC F26 + a16z "renaissance of the American factory") — dropped at screen. Faraday just launched into exactly this, plus heavy forward-deployed ERP integration work; wrong shape for an evenings-and-weekends builder.
5. AI RFQ/drawing-review for job shops and wire-harness makers — dropped at screen. Paperless Parts and Cableteque already sell this exact workflow to this exact buyer with AI drawing reading.
6. Agent permission/access review for mid-market (off the a16z CISO survey: 46% fear agents exceeding permissions) — dropped at screen as both crowded (Token Security, Grip, Obsidian, Nudge, Reco all shipping) and too close to past ideas SkillProof and Driftwatch.
7. Document-parsing QA/regression harness built on LlamaIndex's DPP — dropped at screen. Buyer is a developer, market is the crowded doc-AI tooling space, and it reads as a sibling of past idea EvalSeed.
8. "Plaid for government benefits" document-verification wedge (YC RFS, Gustaf Alströmer) — dropped at screen. Real signal, but the sales cycle is county agencies and the builder has no public-sector route; months to a first dollar.
9. Customer-PO terms and penalty-clause extractor for B2B suppliers (reads the buyer's T&Cs and flags OTIF/chargeback exposure before signing) — finalist, lost to Dockproof. goHeather and contract-AI vendors cover retail/hospitality supplier agreements, and the pain is annual, not weekly.
10. Sales-order entry agent for manufacturers rekeying emailed POs into ERP — dropped at screen. Five AI sales-order-automation tools already compared in trade press; crowded and integration-heavy.
11. Brand-vs-3PL chargeback attribution ledger — merged into Dockproof as the evidence packet. Standalone, the buyer is ambiguous (neither side wants to fund proof that may indict them).

PROJECT
1. Parsedoff — blind A/B of two document parsers on your own page, vote, reveal, DPP rule verdicts, public leaderboard. PICK: the only candidate where the new thing (DPP, 28 Oct) is both the hook and the scoring engine, the input is personal, and the output is an argument.
2. DPP Report Card — upload a page, get a 0-100 score of one parser against all 140 DPP rules. Finalist, lost: one parser means nothing to argue with, and it reads like homework; Parsedoff is the same build with a vote bolted on. Folded in as the reveal panel.
3. Claude Directory Explorer — browse/search every connector in Claude's new directory as a shelf, with permissions surfaced. Dropped at screen: no public dump of the directory to scrape reliably, and awesome-mcp-servers lists already own this shape.
4. Agent-Ready Scanner — paste your URL, see how an agent reads your site. Dropped at screen: dead on arrival, Cloudflare's isitagentready.com plus Frase and BaaDigi all ship free versions already.
5. MCP Tool-Poisoning Peek — paste an MCP server URL, get injection patterns in tool descriptions. Dropped at screen: at least three free versions exist (plat.one/mcp-audit, mcpplaygroundonline.com), and it's close to past ideas SkillPeek/SkillProof.
6. Sol Explainer — type a concept, get a live interactive diagram via gpt-6.1-sol ultrafast. Dropped: checked and real ($12/$60 per M tokens ultrafast — too expensive to run free), and it's a thin clone of the FarzaTV demo in the bookmark, which the rules forbid.
7. Slack-as-Video / UI-to-video — screenshot of an app becomes a narrated product video. Dropped at screen: html-video (4.8k stars), Remotion and HeyGen HyperFrames occupy this; also a heavy render pipeline, not a weekend.
8. Three Clocks — a browsable visual of model vs GPU vs fab release cadences from the @neimuc27 post. Dropped: no clean public dataset for fab/GPU timelines, so it would be hand-curated opinion dressed as data.
9. Grok Shipping Diff — track what AI assistants shipped week over week from public changelogs. Dropped: changelog scraping is brittle and this is close to past idea Driftwatch's territory.
10. Receipt Archaeologist — photo of a receipt becomes an illustrated story of where the money went. Dropped at generate: cute, but a one-time toy with no reason to return and heavy image-gen cost per use.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised faradaycompute.com (Faraday YC F26 — two-person SF team, AI ops agents for manufacturers; killed candidate 4 as too close and too integration-heavy), parseprotocol.com / the LlamaIndex DPP blog (140 parsing rules covering tables, forms, checkboxes, key-value regions — this became the technical "why now" for turning routing guides into structured rules, and killed candidate 7 as a developer-tool sibling of EvalSeed), and the a16z CISO survey (92%/83%/55% production AI adoption, 46% fear agents exceeding permissions, 87% expect 2027 budget rises — real but crowded, and overlapping past ideas SkillProof and Driftwatch, so candidate 6 died).
Screening pot (6/6): manufacturing ERP/BOM cleanup costs; document-parsing accuracy market; non-human-identity and shadow-AI governance (found Token Security, Grip, Obsidian, Nudge, Reco — closed); manufacturing RFQ/drawing review (found Paperless Parts and Cableteque selling this exact workflow — closed); PO terms and vendor-agreement review (found goHeather — closed); sales-order-entry automation for manufacturers (trade press already comparing five AI tools — closed). These six calls eliminated candidates 4-10 and pushed the retail-deduction thread forward as the only one with published penalty dollars.
Deep research pot (12/12): OTIF and retailer deduction economics (Walmart 3% of COGS, Target $0.75/carton ASN with $100 min, routing violations $50-$500/shipment, CRF median 1.1-2% of sales non-trade, SupplyPike's 6.5%-of-invoices claim); the competitor map on both sides of the split (SPS Commerce prevention+recovery with cost/support complaints on G2, Capterra and Trustpilot; SupplyPike $25M Series B / ~$40M total; iNymbus $0.40-0.70/claim; Glimpse; Vendormint; AisleCore $749/$1,699; RetailPath $1.3M pre-seed from Gutter Capital; Crstl with Shopify Ventures participation; Cleo's 2026 Chargeback Prevention); routing-guide revision cadence and notification (no published schedules, portal-only posting — confirms the blind spot but also that nobody can prove a "missed revision" chargeback category); who actually owns the pre-ship check (answer: nobody cleanly — brand ops owns the outcome, 3PL executes, EDI provider only moves documents); 3PL liability allocation and evidence practice (contract-based, ShipMonk sells loadout photos); retailer data access (Retail Link / Partners Online / Vendor Central are portal exports, no public APIs — this is the main plumbing risk and why effort is 3+ months); and market sizing (Kroger's 60,000+ vendors, no clean CPG brand counts, no credible vendor-compliance-software market figure — so market_note is built bottom-up and labelled as estimate).
Sharpening pot (5/5): spent verifying RetailerHub's exact product boundary, published pricing and Version Intel feature; checking whether any 2026 startup closes the deduction-code-to-pre-ship-checklist loop (answer: feasible, no named vendor proven); testing whether recovery tools deliver root cause and fixes (industry guidance recommends it, no vendor proves it, no direct operator quotes found — so pain stayed at 8, not 9); testing 3PL demand for attribution evidence (plausible, contract-driven, ShipMonk precedent — lifted market_pull to 8); and testing demand for a shipment-level compliance evidence packet (practice exists in fragments, no standalone product — supports the wedge). Net effect of sharpening: the idea moved from a document-monitoring tool that RetailerHub already owns to a dock-release gate with an evidence artefact, and the score moved 7.0 to 7.6.
Investor signals weighed: YC's [latest] "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (the warehouse supervisor doing specialist compliance work) and "AI for City Hall" (rejected — past idea Backcheck already occupies it); a16z's [latest] "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data", "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" and "Vertical AI evolves to multiplayer" (the brand+3PL two-sided workflow). Signals set the aim; the scores rest on the deduction economics and the competitor map.
Sharpening (7 to 7.6): Round 1 — weakest criteria: gap 6, wedge 7 (first_score 7.0). Original shape was "parse retailer routing guides into monitored rules and alert on changes." Research (Perplexity on retailerhub.ai, plans page and case studies) found RetailerHub already does precisely that: founded 2024, 1-10 people, bootstrapped, $500-$3,000/mo by retailer count, with a "Version Intel" feature that diffs guide revisions and auto-updates SOPs, plus a GPA Logistics case study across four facilities and 60-70 retailers. That closed the gap on the original idea. Change made: move the wedge off the document and onto the moment of release — a per-PO gate that blocks sign-off on red checks, seeded by the brand's own deduction history, output as a frozen evidence packet. Follow-up research confirmed the reshaped idea sits in open space: RetailerHub's own positioning stops at searchable SOPs and alerts with no shipment enforcement; the recovery vendors (SupplyPike, iNymbus, Glimpse, RetailPath, AisleCore) are post-deduction by their own descriptions; Cleo's 2026 "Chargeback Prevention" flags at-risk orders but is EDI-centric and enterprise; and an explicit search for a startup closing the loop from deduction code to per-PO checklist returned "the workflow is feasible; evidence for startups delivering that exact end-to-end loop is limited." Gap 6 to 7 (not higher — RetailerHub is one product decision away, and I could not get independent confirmation of how far its SOPs go). Wedge 7 to 8: the gate plus packet is a weeks-long one-retailer, one-brand build that a single brand would pay a $1,000/mo pilot for, matching published competitor price points.
Round 2 — weakest remaining: market_pull 7. Change made: add the 3PL as a co-buyer and distribution channel rather than selling only to brands. Research found the liability question is contract-allocated and genuinely contested — retailers deduct from the brand as vendor of record, but 3PL contracts can assign warehouse-caused penalties back to the 3PL, and sources describe disputes collapsing into negotiation when neither side can prove root cause. ShipMonk already markets timestamped freight-loadout photos as chargeback protection, which proves 3PLs will invest in evidence capture. One 3PL sale covers dozens of brands (GPA Logistics: 60-70 retailers across four facilities). Market_pull 7 to 8. I deliberately did not raise pain above 8 or timing above 7: the deduction dollar figures are vendor/industry estimates rather than audited benchmarks, and the 2026 Target/Amazon rule-change dates came from secondary sources I could not verify in the retailer portals.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the DPP/parseprotocol launch (confirmed 140 rules, working draft, MIT code + CC BY 4.0 protocol, downloadable Claude skill — this is what made a rule-citing grader buildable rather than invented); Simulon Reality-Aware Rendering (no public API → killed every AR candidate before I wrote them down); Claude connectors directory (it's the MCP connectors catalog, submissions reviewed — killed the directory-explorer idea since there's no scrapeable public list). A fourth summary on Addy Osmani's article and one on Sol pricing came from the screening pot.
Screening pot (5/5): prior-art checks on parse-comparison tools, generative-UI/Sol demos, the Claude directory, video-as-code, and MCP injection scanners. Killed candidates 3, 5, 6 and 7 outright — the MCP scanner and agent-readiness spaces are already crowded with free tools, and video-as-code has 4.8k-star incumbents.
Deep research pot (8/8): on the two document finalists. Confirmed OCRia-1 + LlamaParse pricing and the free tier (~1,000 pages/month); confirmed Mistral OCR at ~1,000 pages/$; confirmed ParseBench is ~2,000 pages, 130+ models, static, no upload; confirmed Perplexity could find no public blind-vote OCR arena, only PuffinParse (local install, own keys) and Aryn DocParse (single parser, boxes) nearby; confirmed Gemini 3 Flash free tier exists for the judge model. That is what moved this from "another benchmark page" to "the unoccupied arena slot".
Sharpening pot (4/4): checked that no arena-style OCR voting site exists (clear), that no free "RAG read report card" exists (clear — closest is Veryfi's paid API), that browser-direct calls to OpenAI/Mistral are not safe or verified (so: one tiny backend), and searched for an existing DPP-rule linter (nothing found). Net effect: usefulness 5→6, shareability 7→8, buildability 7→8, first_score 7.2 → 7.8.
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: compare once, pick a parser, never return). Change: added the blind vote and a public leaderboard of win rates by document type, so every upload contributes and the page has fresh data each week; added "new model enters the arena" as the recurring reason to come back (ParseBench shows 130+ models and a steady drip of releases — OCRia-1 landed 22 Oct 2026, Mistral OCR 4 earlier). Research: Perplexity found no public OCR equivalent of LMSYS Arena — only private annotator evals inside the Mistral OCR 4 announcement — and ParseBench is a static benchmark with no user upload or vote. So the arena angle is genuinely unoccupied. Usefulness 5 → 6 (still not a weekly habit for most; a leaderboard is a reason to return but an estimated one, so I capped it). Shareability 7 → 8 on the same change: a blind vote + reveal is an argument, and arguments travel.
Round 2 — weak criterion: buildability (7, unchecked). Change: moved all model calls server-side and cut v1 to single-page uploads with a hard daily budget. Research confirmed OpenAI tells you not to put keys in the browser and Mistral's browser CORS support is unverified, so a static page was never viable — one tiny backend it is; and confirmed costs are trivial (Mistral OCR ~1,000 pages/$, LlamaParse free tier ~1,000 pages/month, Gemini 3 Flash free tier), and DPP is MIT/CC BY 4.0 so the rules can be shipped with attribution. Buildability 7 → 8 (not 9: it needs a backend and a budget cap, so it isn't a free static page).
prototype_summary: An interactive Dockproof prototype where a Walmart routing-guide rulebook and past deduction history drive a pre-ship compliance gate that catches $4,540 of chargeback exposure on PO 8842190117 and produces a signed evidence packet.
